summary: Fund

Pabrai Wagons ETF, ticker WAGN, NYSE Arca (it began trading on the NYSE on Feb 9, 2026 ; a June 18, 2026 release announced the move to NYSE Arca). Actively managed, long-only, non-diversified. CUSIP 74316P538.
Manager

Mohnish Pabrai is the sole portfolio manager. The adviser is Dhandho Funds LLC, doing business as Pabrai Wagons Advisors, in West Lake Hills, Texas. The prospectus says the fund depends on him and would have to liquidate without him.
Objective

Long-term capital appreciation: a concentrated portfolio of high-quality businesses bought at a meaningful discount to intrinsic value and held for many years. No geographic or industry limits; up to 100% outside the US, including emerging and frontier markets.
History

Started as the Pabrai Wagons Fund, a mutual fund, on Sep 29, 2023. It converted into the ETF on Feb 6, 2026 (first ETF trade Feb 9) and carries the mutual fund's Institutional Class performance history. The ETF replaced share classes costing 1.25% (retail) and 1.00% (institutional) net.
Fee
0.90% a year, a single flat fee. The adviser pays most operating costs. Brokerage costs, taxes, borrowing interest and acquired-fund fees are excluded. There is no 12b-1 fee and no performance fee.
Size
About $298 million in early November 2026 (the fact sheet shows $313.0 million at its reporting date). Pabrai's firms manage $1.4 billion in total across the private funds and the ETF.
Holdings

20 positions. The top 10 are 67.4% of assets (Oct 31, 2026): Reysas REIT 14.9%, Transocean 9.2%, Warrior Met Coal 7.0%, Edelweiss 5.9%, Gimat 5.8%, Valaris 5.6%, Noble 5.0%, TAV Airports 4.8%, Odfjell Drilling 4.7%, Constellation Software 4.5%. The fund reports zero overlap with the S&P 500.
Sectors

Energy 24.7%, Real Estate 14.9%, Information Technology 14.3%, Financials 13.6%, Industrials 12.3%, Materials 11.4%, Consumer Staples 5.8%, Consumer Discretionary 2.9%, cash 0.2% (Oct 31, 2026). At June 30, 2026 the country split was Turkey 29.7%, US 23.1%, India 13.7%, Switzerland 9.5%, Canada 8.9%, Kazakhstan 4.9%.
Turnover
40% for the year to June 30, 2026 (69.25% the year before).
Shareholders

Held mostly through brokers. As of Oct 7, 2026 record holders over 5%: Charles Schwab 23.81%, National Financial Services 19.32%, Vanguard Brokerage 17.69%, Interactive Brokers 10.12%, Stifel 6.94%, Pershing 5.03%.

stake.answer: Almost nothing, in the ETF itself. The fund's Statement of Additional Information (dated Oct 31, 2026) reports Mohnish Pabrai's ownership in the fund as $1–$10,000 as of June 30, 2026. That is the lowest range the form offers. A year earlier, for the mutual fund, it said he did not beneficially own any shares as of June 30, 2025.
points: Where his money is: he indirectly owns about 19% of the adviser (through Dhandho Holdings), which earns the 0.90% fee, and he gets distributions from it. He also earns a salary and performance fees from Dalal Street, which runs the private Pabrai Investment Funds. Those private funds hold many of the same companies, and the fund documents say his funds own more than 20% of Gimat.
The documents do not say how much of his own wealth sits in the private funds, so his total personal exposure to these same stocks cannot be read from the ETF filings.

Neither the website, the FAQ, the investor presentation nor the 2025 and 2026 shareholder reports mention a personal investment amount. The adviser's regulatory brochure says only that the adviser, its employees or related persons 'may hold an interest in the ETF'.
Trustees: none owns any ETF shares, and trustees and officers as a group own under 1% (as of Sep 30, 2026).

good: Distinct portfolio. Several writers say the holdings are hard to replicate: international value, mostly outside the US, with zero overlap with the S&P 500. (Bezek, Seeking Alpha; ETF Central)

Pedigree and process. A manager who describes himself as a student of Warren Buffett, with a stated discipline of buying great businesses cheaply and holding them for a long time. Supporters like the willingness to hold cash and to hold winners. (Binary Tree Analytics, Seeking Alpha; the fund's own materials)

Cheaper and simpler than the old mutual fund. The ETF costs 0.90% against 1.00%–1.25% net before, with better tax efficiency and intraday trading. The adviser's own presentation and the information statement make this case.
Recent results. 28.90% for the year to June 30, 2026 against 22.32% for the S&P 500, and 30.14% for 2026 through October.
Steady inflows. Data sites show net inflows over the last one and three months and assets roughly doubling in 2026 (about $150 million in March to about $300 million).
bad: The fee. At 0.90% the fund costs far more than index funds (VT is 0.06% on ETF Database's comparison page) and more than the 0.69% average ETF Database shows for its segment. Ian Bezek, a former hedge fund analyst writing on Seeking Alpha in June 2026, called the fee relatively high and said it is only justified if the unique portfolio delivers, which he doubted. He rated the fund bearish.
Concentration and key-man risk. 20 positions and the top ten at 67%, with the prospectus saying the fund would liquidate without Pabrai.
Country and sector bets. Nearly 30% in Turkey, large energy and offshore-drilling exposure, and cyclical coal, all of which can fall together. India and Kazakhstan add governance and currency risk.

Track record. It still trails the S&P 500 since inception (16.91% a year against 21.83% at Oct 31, 2026), and the ETF itself is under a year old. Binary Tree Analytics noted the short history and said it would watch risk-adjusted results.

Trading costs. ETF Database lists an average bid-ask spread of 3.22% and a median premium to NAV of 0.47% with a historical maximum of 1.87%. Treat that as one data point; I could not check how current it is. Use limit orders, as the sponsor's own deck advises.
Promotional material. The ETF Central article on the fund reads as sponsor-written and does not list fees; the valuation claims in the investor presentation are the manager's own.
opinions.note: What I could not find: I searched for Reddit, Bogleheads, Morningstar, Barron's and WSJ commentary on the fund and none came back readable, so the views above come from the two Seeking Alpha articles, ETF Central, ETF Database, the adviser's own documents and the SEC filings. The fee criticism is the main theme found; I did not find anyone arguing the 0.90% fee is low.

history.title: History: the Pabrai Wagons Fund (mutual fund), Sep 29, 2023 to Feb 6, 2026
intro: The Pabrai Wagons Fund opened on September 29, 2023 as a mutual fund run by Mohnish Pabrai with the same approach as today's ETF: a concentrated portfolio of a few high-conviction holdings, anywhere in the world. It had two share classes, Retail (WAGNX) and Institutional (WGNIX). Retail carried a 0.25% 12b-1 fee and a 0.10% servicing fee, Institutional the 0.10% servicing fee only, and both charged a 1.00% fee on shares sold within 90 days. The adviser capped expenses at 1.25% (Retail) and 1.00% (Institutional) net; before the cap they were 1.84% and 1.59% in the year to June 2025.

It started small: net assets were $32.4 million at June 30, 2024 and $78.9 million at June 30, 2025 (both classes). Brokerage platforms held nearly all of it; at Sep 30, 2025 Vanguard Brokerage held 52.96% of the Institutional class, Schwab 21.19% and National Financial Services 20.74%. The largest single position was an Indian financial company, Edelweiss, at about 20% of the fund when it was bought.
why: Growth. The fund and adviser said the ETF would reach more investors. Pabrai said the mutual fund would not be profitable for the adviser until about $150 million of assets (he said the fund was about $80 million in August 2025). The documents do not tie the conversion to that number, but it shows why growth mattered.

Tax efficiency. ETFs can meet redemptions by handing over shares instead of selling them, which usually means fewer capital-gains distributions. The mutual fund had paid $0.14 a share in capital gains for the year to June 2025. The fund's FAQ says the ETF also uses tax-loss harvesting.

Lower and simpler cost. One 0.90% fee replaced the 1.25% (Retail) and 1.00% (Institutional) net expense ratios, and the ETF drops the 1.00% short-term redemption fee. The information statement shows $92 a year on $10,000 for the ETF against $127 for Retail and $102 for Institutional, and says the adviser could not recoup earlier fee waivers from the ETF.

Trading and transparency. Intraday trading at market prices, and daily holdings disclosure. The FAQ says Pabrai spent most of a 28-year career running private funds for institutions and the ETF extends the strategy to a broader audience.

What shareholders gave up, which the information statement also lists: the ability to redeem directly at NAV, and brokerage costs and bid-ask spreads when trading. ETF shares can also trade above or below NAV.
history.after: Since the conversion the record has been much better (28.90% for the year to June 30, 2026 against 22.32% for the index) and assets have roughly doubled to about $300 million. The documents do not say the conversion caused either; the period also coincided with strong gains in his energy and coal holdings.

YCharts shows about $174 million of net inflows over the past year, so most of the growth appears to be new money rather than gains.

stocks.name: TAV Airports
notes: Sep 2024: one of the three Turkish names he called among his highest-conviction ideas; much of the revenue is euro-denominated or earned outside Turkey, so it is ring-fenced from Turkish political risk.
May 2025: the bet is bottom-up, not on Turkey. TAV earns mostly euros against lira costs, so inflation is a tailwind.

Mar 2025: called management among the best he has met, and described the Almaty airport (bought for about $300 million, EBITDA possibly over $200 million a year). Edelweiss and TAV were each about 15% to 16% of the fund at the end of 2024.
Mar 2026: mostly hard-currency revenue; about 46% owned by the French government.

Jun 2026: down about 30% in dollars over two years because of Pratt & Whitney engine groundings, Boeing delivery delays and very low per-passenger fees at Almaty. He expects those to ease in two to three years and stayed bullish.

Sep 2026: agreed it is not comparable to Heathrow or Paris and that geopolitics has hurt. Low-cost carriers use gates efficiently; at Almaty TAV gave up fuel income in return for much higher per-passenger fees, which he expects to show in 2027 results. TAV is paying out cash and may buy more assets.
stocks.desc: Turkish airport operator that runs Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Antalya and other terminals, plus airports in Georgia, Tunisia, Saudi Arabia, North Macedonia and Almaty, Kazakhstan. Earns fees per passenger plus duty-free and services, much of it in euros.

stocks.name: Anadolu Efes
notes: Mar 2024: owns 50% of Coca-Cola Icecek, yet he wanted both so Efes alone would not dilute his Icecek exposure. He praised the family's reputation (it owns McDonald's Turkey) and AB InBev handing its 50% of the Russian beer business to Efes for no upfront money (valued at about $1.2 billion).
Sep 2024: beer volumes in Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere are ring-fenced from Turkey.
Mar 2025: fell out after Russia took over the assets of its Russian brewing joint venture on Dec 31, 2024; he moved it to the too-hard pile.
stocks.desc: Turkish brewer and Coca-Cola bottler holding company. It makes Efes beer in Turkey and parts of Europe and Central Asia and owns half of Coca-Cola Icecek.

stocks.name: Coca-Cola Icecek
notes: Mar 2024: the world's third-largest Coke bottler, which could win part of India or Bangladesh. The Uzbekistan bottler was bought at about 25 times EBITDA with Coke selling its share cheaply; net income quadrupled in a year.

Sep 2024: among his highest conviction. Boycotts are hard to handicap and he would not sell because of them; he praised the brand, management and the CEO. Uzbekistan deal: about $300 million paid for about $20 million of pretax earnings, now over $100 million.
May 2025: said it only looked sold in the filings in some months because it can fall outside the disclosed top ten.
stocks.flag: The Jun 30, 2024 schedule lists 130,150 shares for $3.29 million, which would be about $25 a share. That does not fit the later schedules (about $1.4 to $1.7), so I use Sep 30, 2024 as the first price.
stocks.desc: Turkey-based bottler and distributor of Coca-Cola drinks across Turkey, Pakistan, Central Asia and the Middle East. One of the largest Coke bottlers in the world.

stocks.name: AG Anadolu Grubu Holding
notes: Listed with the Turkish allocation in the first annual letter (Anadolu Grubu). I found no specific remarks about it on the calls.
stocks.desc: Turkish conglomerate holding company with stakes in Anadolu Efes, Migros supermarkets, Anadolu Isuzu trucks and other businesses.

stocks.name: Edelweiss Financial Services
notes: He has owned it and Nuvama for almost ten years; Nuvama was spun out of Edelweiss. Early on it was about 20% of the fund and the largest position.

May 2025: he avoids levered financials, but most of Edelweiss's lending is in run-off and most of its businesses are not lending. Market cap about $1 billion versus about $2.5 billion for the Nuvama wealth business it spun out. He expects four or five spin-offs in four or five years and wants to keep the spun-off shares.
Mar 2025: with TAV, his two highest-conviction ideas; the alternative-assets arm (EAAA) was expected to list at $1 billion to $1.5 billion.
Jun 2026: Nuvama's market cap now exceeds Edelweiss's; an IPO of EAAA is planned within months. One of two co-CEOs there recently left, which he called not good news, but the thesis stands.
Sep 2026: sees Indian financial services as early-stage, like the US around 1980 to 1982, and compares it with buying Schwab then.
stocks.desc: Indian financial group in alternative asset management, credit, insurance and wealth. It has been spinning off units such as Nuvama, and an asset-management arm is expected to list.

stocks.name: Nuvama Wealth Management
notes: Spun out of Edelweiss. May 2025: worth about $2.5 billion against Edelweiss at about $1 billion. Sep 2026: same Indian financial-services thesis as Edelweiss.
stocks.desc: Indian wealth, asset-services and capital-markets firm spun out of Edelweiss and listed in 2025. It serves wealthy and institutional clients.

stocks.name: Reysas Logistics
notes: He and his funds own about 30% across everything, a cap he set himself after a founder hinted discomfort with more. That cap is why WAGN holds little of it. He says Logistics is the cheaper bet, trading below the value of the REIT shares it owns.
No investor relations or deck (Mar 2026, Jun 2026); he is fine with it because the father-son team are exceptional capital allocators requiring 25% to 35% annual returns.
May 2025: over six years the lira lost more than 80% while Reysas's intrinsic value in dollars doubled or tripled. Aug 2025: held since 2019 and showed little return for three or four years.
Mar 2024: called out the aggregate ownership limit across all his accounts; Mar 2025: a founder's body language meant it would not be a big WAGN position.
stocks.noteFirst: The Dec 31, 2024 schedule row for this name is partly garbled in my read; I treat it as Reysas Logistics.
stocks.desc: Turkish logistics and warehousing company run by a father-son team, which develops and operates warehouses and also owns shares in Reysas REIT.

stocks.name: Reysas Gayrimenkul (REIT)
notes: Sep 2026: his highest-conviction idea; he would sell only if the family sold. His funds own a little over 12%. About 15% of WAGN is the REIT. He calls it a compounder, not a REIT.

Mar 2026: when he first visited, market cap was about $15 million versus $600 million to $800 million of liquidation value. Footprint about 12 million square feet, going to about 23 million in three years.

Sep 2026 examples of the family's creativity: a former Tata factory (over 1 million square feet) being redeveloped into warehouses, and a government-matched organic tomato farm for Germany. Jun 2026: he warned he mostly gives the bull case and some holdings will lose.
stocks.noteFirst: The Jun 30, 2025 schedule row was not captured in my read; the fund held it then.
stocks.desc: Turkish real estate investment trust that owns and rents out logistics warehouses and land, with inflation-linked leases. A sister company of Reysas Logistics.

stocks.name: Gimat
notes: Jun 2026: buying began in 2025; across everything he manages he owns over 25%. At purchase the market cap was about $70 million to $80 million and the real estate alone was about $70 million. A venture-style bet on growing beyond two stores; he compared it to Walmart and See's Candies and said not adding would have been a cardinal sin. Market cap now over $300 million.
Mar 2026: he will not be an activist. Downside is protected by a modest entry valuation and real estate it plans to monetize.

Sep 2026: disappointed that the founder owns under 1% and is paid little. He has urged him, last year and this year, to raise his pay and find a way to give himself shares or options, with no movement. He is not worried: a servant leader, not money-motivated. No concern about unfair treatment of minority shareholders.
stocks.flag: Share count rose about 3x between Dec 2025 and Mar 2026 while the price fell, which looks like a bonus issue or split, so the implied price is not like for like across that date.
stocks.desc: Turkish retailer building a wholesale-club chain. It has two stores today and owns valuable real estate.

stocks.name: TAB Gida
notes: Mar 2026: master franchisee of Burger King and Popeyes in Turkey. Revenue is in lira, which he accepts because management is a "jockey bet" (civil engineers who beat McDonald's).
Sep 2026: expects GLP-1 drugs to hurt it in Turkey as elsewhere. Excited about its Doner brand in China and urged management to copy Chipotle. One of his lowest-conviction holdings.
stocks.desc: Turkish master franchisee of Burger King and Popeyes, with a growing Doner restaurant brand in China.

stocks.name: Kaspi.kz
notes: Mar 2026: "heads I win, tails I do not lose much." The price fell after a dividend cut tied to buying a Turkish fintech and bank. Turkey is seven or eight times Kazakhstan's market and far less digital; the founder is "a total rock star".

Jun 2026: a good team replicating its Kazakhstan playbook in Turkey; dividend reinstated, yielding about 10%. Turkey is a moonshot on top of a business he paid a fair price for. He named Kaspi the likely second-best management team.
Sep 2026: opportunistic, not part of an emerging-markets theme. Kaspi owns 92% to 93% of Hepsiburada and he expects it to take it private. He expects clearer results in one to three years.
stocks.desc: Kazakhstan fintech super-app combining payments, online marketplace and consumer lending. It is expanding into Turkey and owns most of Hepsiburada.

stocks.name: Transocean
notes: Mar 2026: called the acquisition of Valaris a stroke of genius: leverage falls, the larger footprint helps contract negotiations and Transocean is the stronger operator.

Jun 2026: with Noble and Valaris, over 19% of the fund. Capital-intensive can be excellent (Micron, FlightSafety, BNSF) if bought well below replacement cost; the last drillship ever built has already been built. A big win-win with little spread.

Sep 2026: agreed debt is a concern, but management dislikes it and has cut it sharply. He praised the equity issuance at about $3 a share, expects the Valaris deal to close in Q4 and leverage to be a non-issue by the end of 2027. He acknowledged going "out on a limb".
stocks.desc: Offshore drilling contractor that owns and operates deepwater rigs and drillships rented to oil companies. Heavily indebted, and buying Valaris.

stocks.name: Valaris
notes: May 2025: the offshore group (Valaris, Noble, Tidewater) emerged from restructuring with little debt. Replacement cost could be five to ten times market cap, new drillships would need day rates 50% to 100% higher, and offshore all-in costs of $30 to $50 a barrel beat shale.
Mar and Jun 2026: Transocean's purchase of Valaris is a win-win; Valaris is underlevered.
stocks.desc: Offshore drilling contractor with a large fleet of drillships and jack-up rigs, which emerged from bankruptcy in 2021 with little debt. Being acquired by Transocean.

stocks.name: Noble Corp.
notes: May 2025: traded at about five times non-peak cash flow with a dividend yield approaching 10%. Jun 2026: counted in the over 19% offshore drilling weight; no plan to exit soon.
stocks.noteFirst: The Sep 30, 2025 row was not captured in my read; the fund appears to have held it then.
stocks.desc: Offshore drilling contractor renting floating rigs and jack-ups to oil producers worldwide. Emerged from restructuring with low debt and pays a dividend.

stocks.name: Tidewater
notes: May 2025: one of the three offshore names that emerged from restructuring with little debt (see Valaris). I found no other specific remarks.
stocks.desc: Operator of offshore support vessels that supply and service oil platforms and rigs. Restructured out of bankruptcy in 2017.

stocks.name: Warrior Met Coal
notes: May 2025: his favorite met coal bet: a low-cost operator that was not losing money in a trough, lower still once Blue Creek came online.

Mar 2026: he rejects the cyclical-versus-compounder labels and compares it to Saudi Aramco. At $220 a ton for a year he put Warrior at over $550 million of cash flow against a market cap under $5 billion. A tax-loss rule capped any holder at 5% and blocked buybacks until Apr 19, 2026.
Jun 2026: cost to the port $15 to $30 a ton versus roughly $25 to $60 for Alpha; he would rank it higher even if it paid only dividends.
Sep 2026: all longwall, nearer the port and able to ship by barge or rail, so it pays the railroad under half of what Alpha pays; near the bottom of the seaborne cost curve.
stocks.desc: Alabama producer of metallurgical coal used to make steel, shipped through the Port of Mobile. It uses longwall mining and is developing the Blue Creek mine.

stocks.name: Alpha Metallurgical Resources
notes: May 2025: no disagreement with management stopping buybacks to keep about $450 million in cash. His case rests on the end state: if shares fall from 12 to 13 million to about 3 million in 20 years while earning $1 billion to $1.5 billion a year, that is about $500 a share of cash flow. He hoped coal prices stayed depressed so buybacks stay cheap.

Mar 2026: cut the share count about 32% over four years; he sketched a path to about $180, then a dividend payer, possibly over $250 in seven or eight years. What he watches is shares outstanding in 2035. India's steel demand rising around 2028 to 2029 is the turn.
Jun and Sep 2026: second to Warrior; depends on one railroad that takes roughly a quarter of the coal price, up to about $60 a ton, but its many small mines make its reserves in effect near-endless.
stocks.noteFirst: The Jun 30, 2025 value in my read was garbled, so that quarter is skipped.
stocks.desc: US producer of metallurgical coal used in steelmaking, mined in Appalachia from many small mines. It has been shrinking its share count through buybacks.

stocks.name: Arch Resources
notes: Mar 2024: one of the four coal names. Sep 2024: surprised but pleased by the Arch and CONSOL merger; a combined company of about $5 billion market cap could make about $500 million of cash in a bad year and over $1 billion in a good one, with buybacks the only use of cash.
stocks.desc: US coal producer focused on metallurgical coal, with a thermal-coal business in Wyoming. Merged with CONSOL in early 2025 to form Core Natural Resources.

stocks.name: CONSOL Energy
notes: Mar 2024: the only thermal holding; exports most of its coal, a lot for industrial use, forward sells 12 to 18 months with price bands, has no meaningful debt.

Mar 2025: he sold Core Natural Resources (the Arch-CONSOL merger, a mix of thermal and met coal) to hold a pure met coal portfolio, keeping Warrior and Alpha. Mar 2026: he declined thermal coal again because of the Iran war.
stocks.desc: US coal miner that mainly sells thermal coal, much of it exported, from its Pennsylvania mining complex. Merged with Arch in early 2025.

stocks.name: Occidental Petroleum
notes: Sep 2024: a placeholder with low downside, under 4% of the fund, run by Vicki Hollub. Mar 2025: one of his lower-conviction bets, a bet on Hollub. May 2025: likes her but prefers simpler, smaller businesses.
Dec 2025 and Mar 2026: listed among his lowest-conviction ideas, sold and replaced by higher-conviction ones.
stocks.desc: Large US oil and gas producer with chemicals and carbon-capture businesses. Run by CEO Vicki Hollub.

stocks.name: Mongolian Mining
notes: Sep 2026: sold because Mongolian government factions want to revisit the mining deal terms, which he called an existential threat he could not handicap. He still liked the business (a surface coal mine, and a gold side that did far better than designed, with gold at about $5,000 an ounce).
stocks.desc: Hong Kong-listed Mongolian miner of coking coal (surface mine) and a gold business, selling mostly to Chinese steelmakers.

stocks.name: Danaos
notes: Sep 2024: his only Greek position, with cash flows locked in by long charters. May 2025: it only looked sold in the filings because it fell outside the disclosed top ten.

Sep 2026: met senior management in Athens and his view rose. He began buying in the $70s to $80s a share less than a year earlier; the stock is now more than twice that and still deeply below net asset value. Low-cost, light-covenant ship financing via Japanese vehicles. "A special company, not a typical Greek shipper."
stocks.desc: Greek-run owner of container ships that charters them to shipping lines on long contracts. Financing is unusually cheap thanks to Japanese lenders.

stocks.name: Euroseas
notes: I found no specific remarks about it.
stocks.desc: Greek owner of small and mid-size container ships chartered to shipping lines.

stocks.name: Daqo New Energy
notes: I found no specific remarks about it (listed in the first letter's China exposure).
stocks.desc: Chinese maker of polysilicon, the raw material for solar panels.

stocks.name: Constellation Software
notes: Mar 2026: the stock fell from about $5,500 to the low $2,000s. He argued AI helps incumbents in vertical-market software; acquisition multiples (historically 4 to 5 times cash flow) could fall. No manager escapes a high miss rate.

Jun 2026: P/E is the wrong lens because of non-cash goodwill charges; organic growth about 3% a year deserves a cash-flow multiple of 10 to 17 times; the second engine is buying businesses at 4 or 5 times cash flow. He calls it the best-managed holding.
Sep 2026: sad about Mark Leonard's health, which led him to leave the board, but the culture is firmly built in.
stocks.noteFirst: The Mar 2024 call lists it as held at Dec 31, 2023, and it appears as about 0.0% in the first letter's Jun 30, 2024 table; the schedules I read show it again from Mar 31, 2026.
stocks.desc: Canadian company that buys and holds thousands of small vertical-market software businesses. Led by founder Mark Leonard until he stepped back from the board.

stocks.name: Lumine Group
notes: Part of the Mark Leonard complex (Constellation, Topicus, Lumine). No separate remarks beyond the Constellation comments.
stocks.noteFirst: The Jun 30, 2026 share count was not readable, so no implied price.
stocks.desc: Canadian spin-off of Constellation Software that buys telecom and media software businesses.

stocks.name: Topicus.com
notes: Mar 2024: held a small piece. Mar 2026: similar DNA to Constellation in a less competitive European market, nothing he does not like.
stocks.noteFirst: A small holding in Jun 2024, absent from the schedules for Sep 2024 to Dec 2025, then re-bought by Mar 2026.
stocks.desc: Dutch spin-off of Constellation Software that buys vertical-market software companies in Europe.

stocks.name: Tiny
notes: One of the tech holdings in the Mar 2024 call grouping; no specific remarks.
stocks.flag: Implied price looks unreliable for this tiny position, so I do not show one.
stocks.desc: Canadian holding company that buys and runs small internet and technology businesses.

stocks.name: Sygnity
notes: I found no specific remarks about it.
stocks.desc: Polish IT services and software company.

stocks.name: Amazon
notes: Mar 2024: relatively low-conviction; mutual fund diversification rules explain the small stake. Its trailing P/E is meaningless because it reinvests heavily.
stocks.desc: US online retailer and cloud-computing company (Amazon Web Services).

stocks.name: Microsoft

stocksNote: Dates and prices come only from the fund’s quarter-end schedules of investments (Jun 30, 2024 through Jun 30, 2026). The fund does not publish trade dates or trade prices, so ‘first seen’ means the first quarter-end schedule where the stock appears, and ‘sold’ means it was gone by the next schedule. The price shown is the implied price at that quarter-end: the reported value divided by the reported shares, in US dollars. It is not what the fund paid or received. Real entry points were sometimes earlier and exits sometimes later. The Mar 31, 2024 and Dec 31, 2023 schedules are not included here, so names held at launch show Jun 30, 2024 as their first look. Three early names (Brookfield, First Citizens, Restaurant Brands) appear only in the first letter or proxy record. The Sep 30, 2026 schedule was not yet published.
themes: Hold a few great businesses for a very long time

The first annual letter says great results come from a few great investments held very long, so the aim is to find them and not sell them, ‘circling the wagons’ around the best ideas. Since about 2017 to 2018 he no longer sells at fair value and may sell only far above it. He says holdings often need five years or more to pay off, and calls the fund’s first two years of underperformance worse than he expected.
Buy far below what the assets are worth

His recurring test is downside protection: ‘heads I win, tails I do not lose much’. Examples he gives are Reysas (market cap about $15 million when he first visited against $600 to $800 million of liquidation value), Gimat (market cap about equal to its real estate), offshore drillers below replacement cost, and Danaos below net asset value. He says ‘micro trumps macro’ and that his Turkey and India positions are bottom-up bets, not country calls.

Much of the case rests on people: the Reysas father and son, Mark Leonard at Constellation, the Kaspi founder, the Edelweiss and Nuvama managers, and buyback-minded coal managers. He openly accepts weaknesses such as no investor relations at Reysas, a Gimat founder who owns under 1%, and lira revenue at TAB Gida.
Reject the cyclical versus compounder labels

He calls Warrior his Aramco, a low-cost producer that rarely loses money, and Reysas REIT a compounder, not a REIT. Capital intensity is fine if bought well below replacement cost (Micron, FlightSafety, BNSF, the last drillship ever built). He insists the coal holdings are metallurgical coal, not a bet on a price spike.
Emerging markets with hard-currency or inflation-linked earnings

He argues TAV earns mostly euros against lira costs, Reysas’s warehouses are inflation-indexed, and over six years the lira lost more than 80% while Reysas’s dollar value doubled or tripled. He says Turkey felt like the US in the 1960s. Kaspi is a Kazakhstan business with a Turkey option on top, and Indian financial services is early-stage, like the US in the early 1980s.
Low interest in the S&P 500 and the Magnificent Seven

He repeatedly compares the S&P 500’s trailing P/E (27.2 to 27.5, against 25.6 in Sep 2000) with the portfolio’s 7.5 to 9, and expects the index’s heavy mega-cap tech weighting to struggle over 10 to 15 years. He accepts the fund trails since inception and says he expects to beat it over the long term with no guarantee.

He says he sold his lowest-conviction names (Occidental, the car dealers, the homebuilders) to fund higher-conviction ones, and sold Anadolu Efes after Russia took its joint venture assets and Mongolian Mining over government risk. He expects only two or three new ideas a year and says he cannot find 20 to 30 great ideas, which makes the fund’s diversification rules a cost.
Fund structure and honesty about the limits

He says mutual fund rules forced baskets (one coal bet, one dealer, one builder would be his choice), that the fund needs about $150 million to cover its costs, and that in hindsight he might have started as an ETF. Daily inflows are allocated by his team by conviction and position limits. He warns that he mostly gives the bull case and that some holdings will lose.
issues: The fee

0.90% is far above index funds. Seeking Alpha’s Ian Bezek (Jun 2026) called it relatively high and justified only if the unique portfolio delivers, which he doubted, and rated the fund bearish. I found no one arguing it is low. On the calls, investors asked about fees and Pabrai said fees could fall with scale, and that the fund would need several billion dollars to cut materially.
Concentration and key-man risk

20 or so positions with the top ten near two-thirds of assets, and the prospectus says the fund would liquidate without Pabrai. Pabrai’s answer is that results come from his top 12 to 15 bets and the fund may fall when markets fall.
Track record

The fund still trails the S&P 500 since inception (16.91% a year against 21.83% to Oct 31, 2026). Shareholders asked on the Mar 2025 call how he explains losing all gains since inception; he said the fund optimises for the long term and does not hedge. Analysts note the ETF is under a year old.
Turkey, geopolitics and currency

Nearly 30% in Turkey. Investors raised the Istanbul mayor’s arrest and lira drop, Coca-Cola Icecek boycotts, and the Russia seizure at Anadolu Efes. Questions on TAV cited the Iran and Ukraine wars, engine groundings, Boeing delays and low Almaty fees, and that it is not comparable to Heathrow or Paris.
Cyclical bets: coal and offshore drilling

Analysts and callers flag that coal, offshore drillers and shipping can fall together. Specific questions: why Alpha bought back stock at $215 to $400 when it was near $120; whether over 19% in offshore drilling is too much; Warrior against Alpha spreads; thermal coal after the Iran war.
Transocean debt and the Valaris deal

A caller on the Sep 2026 call called Transocean’s debt a concern; Pabrai agreed, said management is cutting it, and expects leverage to be a non-issue by the end of 2027, acknowledging he is ‘out on a limb’.
Governance at the smaller Turkish holdings

Questions on Gimat: why the founder owns under 1% and whether minority holders are treated fairly. Reysas gives no investor disclosure. Pabrai says he has no concern on minority treatment and is comfortable with Reysas because of the family’s record.
Conflicts with his private funds

He runs private funds paying performance fees. The adviser’s own filing says this creates an incentive to steer the best ideas to them, with trades allocated by a rotation (Wagons gets priority every fifth day). His own stake in the ETF is $1 to $10,000 as of Jun 30, 2026. His funds own over 25% of Gimat and about 30% of Reysas Logistics, which caps what WAGN can hold.
ETF trading costs and flows

ETF Database shows a wide average spread and a median premium to NAV of about 0.5%; use limit orders. Pabrai said new money is allocated daily on conviction and position limits and he has felt no discomfort with the inflows.
Valuation of the software holdings

On the Mar and Jun 2026 calls he was asked about Constellation’s P/E and about AI risk to vertical-market software. He answered that P/E is the wrong lens (goodwill charges), organic growth deserves a 10 to 17 times cash-flow multiple, and AI should help incumbents.
Kaspi and India
Kaspi’s dividend was cut to fund a Turkish fintech and bank purchase, then reinstated. India carries governance, liquidity and capital-gains tax accrual risks named in the fund’s own risk list.
